title: Configuration Technical Reference
readerIntent: Locate authoritative configuration contracts and extension boundaries.
priorKnowledge: Read the configuration overview and runtime pages.
summary: Technical ownership is distributed across startup configuration, module configuration, topology, tenant properties, and explicitly governed runtime contracts.

sections.heading: Layer resolution
items: Configuration loads through one authoritative layered process from framework and module defaults through project, environment, server, node, tenant, and supported runtime scopes.
Later eligible layers override earlier values while provenance records where an effective value came from. Missing required configuration fails with a clear safe diagnostic.
Environment and topology selection use canonical runtime identity so same-named servers or nodes cannot cross local, development, preproduction, or production.
Later layers are deltas, not copied snapshots. If the earlier owning module already supplies the required value, the later properties.js omits it and inherits it.

sections.heading: Properties and metadata
items: properties.js holds application and module behavior such as timeouts, TTLs, policy mappings, feature activation, endpoints, and provider selection.
package.json remains standard package metadata plus limited module metadata; it does not hold BackOffice, publishing, cache, security, or other runtime behavior.
Secrets are opaque references resolved by governed process or vault integration and never committed, logged, returned to browsers, or persisted in snapshots.

sections.heading: Customization and runtime governance
items: Partners reuse defaults, override properties in customer layers, extend existing definitions, and add a new loader only after a duplication and authority audit.
Runtime change applies only to declared contracts with validation, authorization, preview, immutable approval, activation, audit, concurrency, and rollback.
Changing source configuration and changing a governed runtime snapshot are distinct lifecycles with explicit precedence and restart behavior.

sections.heading: Verification and operations
items: Test default, override, missing, invalid, duplicate, ambiguous topology, tenant isolation, secret failure, restart, runtime activation, stale revision, and rollback.
Provide safe effective-configuration reports with provenance and masking; never expose credentials or protected security internals through public health endpoints.
Document each property purpose, type, default, scope, mutability, security, example, dependency, operational impact, and deprecation.

sections.heading: Authoritative locations
items: config/properties.js: configurable application and module behavior.
config/config.js: loader and configuration-definition contracts where owned by the framework.
Environment, server, and node modules: topology composition and selection.
Tenant or customer property layers: supported business-scope variation.
Runtime-governance schemas, services, interceptors, and audit records: approved mutable contracts.
package.json: standard package and limited module metadata, not general application configuration.

sections.heading: Non-negotiable boundaries
items: Do not create duplicate loaders or parallel authority paths.
Do not copy unchanged module defaults, disabled-provider placeholders, or complete capability policy blocks into project, environment, server, or node configuration.

Servers define process composition, ports, remote coordinates, and intentional process selections; nodes define instance identity and instance-specific differences. Neither becomes a second owner of reusable capability policy.
Do not put credentials or secrets in committed properties.
Do not convert executable business logic into unvalidated data.
Do not treat root docs/ as runtime configuration.
Do not allow runtime mutation of a contract that has no validation, authorization, audit, and rollback design.
